newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION - INDIA'S MARKET STRATEGY - BY KOTAK SECURITIES.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - INDIA'S MARKET STRATEGY - BY KOTAK SECURITIES.

text.p: In a November market strategy report on India, Kotak

Securities' head of research Rajashekar Iyer sees a strong possibility of a market revival as the liquidity situation improves, markets shift focus to fiscal 1996/97 and political developments reduce the influence of communist parties.
MARKET DURING OCTOBER:

The market performed poorly in October and closed about 2.3 percent lower over the previous month. This was despite the improved flow of foreign investment in October compared to the preceding two months.

At $222 million FII investments were still substantially below the very high levels recorded in the January-July period when they averaged $340 million per month but showed progressive improvement from August ($81 million) and September ($123 million).
Amongst domestic institutions only the Life Insurance Corporation of India was a significant buyer and the Unit Trust of India (UTI) appeared to be selling less than it had in previous months.
UTI indicated that it had mobilised 12 billion rupees in the quarter ended December and has set a modest target of 100 billion for its fiscal year ending June 1997.
The positive news is that redemption pressures on the Unit Trust of India (which holds an estimated 9 percent of the market capitalisation) appear to have eased off.
UTI chairman, Jagdish Capoor indicated that redemption pressure which was high in fiscal 1996 (108 billion rupees) and in fiscal 1995 (125 billion rupees) was easing from July.

He attributed the heavy pressure of redemptions in the past two years to redemptions made by corporate investors under pressure because of tight liquidity conditions and tax law changes that made units less attractive to corporate holders of units.

However the controversy surrounding Canbank Mutual Fund's inability to meet its repurchase obligation on the Canstar scheme (the fund had promised to repurchase 10 rupees units issued in November 1990 at 23 rupees in November 1996) has cast a cloud on investor comfort with mutual fund schemes.
It will be a while before the domestic mutual funds regain investor confidence.

Individual investor sentiment towards the market continues to be very subdued. There is little possibility of a significant revival in the next few months in the light of large losses made by individual investors over the past two years, the controversy surrounding management improprieties allegedly committed by large companies like ITC and Shaw Wallace, and UTI's announced plan to prune its portfolio size.

UTI's decision, if implemented, will result in further losses on small stocks - the segment in which the individual investor has lost heavily in the last two years. The market thus continues to be dependent on foreign fund investments to a very large degree.
CORPORATE RESULTS:
The poor performance of the market was despite better-than-expected performance by large corporates like Tata Steel, Tata Engineering, Reliance Industries, Bajaj Auto and SKF Bearings.
Centre for Monitoring the Indian Economy (CMIE) figures indicated a sharp fall in growth in profit after tax in the first half of fiscal 1997.
The study, based on results announcements of 66 companies, indicated that growth rate in PAT was 16 percent compared to 35 percent recorded in the corresponding period of the previous year.
The CMIE study also indicates that higher inventories and trade receivables resulted in interest cost going up by 33 percent - the highest recorded in six years.
Our own study on 35 companies, indicates a similar trend. Interestingly the study indicates a rosier picture on the front of margin growth.
PBDIT (before other income) as a percentage of sales at 19.1 percent shows a sharp improvement compared to corresponding prior period (18.4 percent) and preceding six months (17.2 percent).
Clearly profitability is improving but profit growth has slowed down because of higher interest, depreciation and tax burden.
ECONOMIC INDICATORS:
CMIE figures indicate a 5 percent growth in industrial output in the five months to August 1996 compared to 11.1 percent (revised) grwoth rate recorded in fiscal 1996.
Industrial slowdown is also indicated in exports growth rate at 10 percent in first half of fiscal 1997 compared to 20 percent recorded in fiscal 1997.
Overall imports growth in the first half was 5.2 percent which includes 42 percent growth in petroleum products and decline in non-oil imports.

Non-foods credit of scheduled commercial banks at end-September was 2,425 billion rupees which is around the same level as at March 1996 (2,423 billion rupees). September figures alone however indicate some improvement.
The three important reasons for industrial slowdown are:
** Lack of credit availability and high interest rates.
** Weak demand growth for output of industrial sector following the 0.2 percent growth recorded in agriculture in fiscal 1996.
** Power supply problems - power generation recorded only 2.6 percent growth in the first half compared to 11 percent recorded in the corresponding period in the previous year.
There are distinct indications/possibilities of improvement in each of these factors in the second half of fiscal 1997.

RBI's credit policy announcement in October has led to all round cuts in interest rates and a further reduction in CRR, promised in January, will keep up downward pressure on interest rates and increase money supply to small and medium sized businesses.

Agricultural production is expected to record 4.7 percent growth in fiscal 1997 compared to the meagre 0.9 percent growth rate (revised) recorded in fiscal 1996. This should boost demand from the rural sector.

While there are no indications on improvement in power supply, good monsoon is expected to lead to improvement in hydel power generation (over 20 percent of total power generation) in the second half of the year.
Hydel power generation had declined by 8.7 percent in the first half compared to 5.8 percent growth recorded in thermal and nuclear power.
GOVERNMENT POLICY:
With all its constraints, government policy is focussed on making serious efforts to revive growth rate and capital markets.

The finance minister has mounted substantial pressure on banks and financial institutions to increase supply and lower cost of funds to industry. The effects of these are bound to be seen over the next few months.

Also the government has been aggressively promoting foreign direct investment (FDI). While policy measures to promote FDI should help in the longer term, the short term already indicates a very positive trend.
FDI in the first five months of fiscal 1997 (up to August 1996) at 35 billion rupees was up 46 percent over corresponding previous year.

The August 1996 figure of FDI was the largest ever recorded in a single month so far. Total FDI proposals cleared in the first five months of fiscal 1997 was 126 billion rupees - up 65 percent compared to the previous year.

Interestingly over 75 percent of the total FDI clearances in the first five months were made in July and August. The industries ministry has indicated that as of October the Foreign Investment Promotion Board has cleared all proposals pending when the new government was formed in July.
Government policy tilt is thus extremely favourable towards speeding up industrial growth and lends credence to CMIE's estimate to pick up in growth rate in the second half.
Combined with better growth rate recorded in agriculture the overall GDP growth rate could perk up in the second half.
POLITICAL OUTLOOK:

Political equations in Delhi are being recast with more ex-Congressmen returning to the fold. The changing political scene is putting more pressure on the UF government to toe the Congress line and could lead to either the Congress joining the government or trying to form a government with support from other groups.
While this may be destabilising in the short term it will have no negative impact on government economic policy which should be oriented to acceleration of the industrial growth rate.

The growing influence of the Congress is generally positive as it minimises the risk of the communists, who are unhappy on the government policy towards foreign investment, pressing for a slowdown in foreign investment clearances.
TO SUM UP:
Demand-supply balance for stocks continues to be heavily influenced by FII investments which have slowed down since July. However conditions are ambient for pick-up in foreign investment.
While the BSE 30-share index is near its lowest level of the past two years there are a number of POSITIVE FACTORS:
** Interest rates are declining and credit availability is easing for small/medium sized businesses.
** Agricultural production growth (forecast at 4.7 percent against 0.9 percent in fiscal 1996 should stimulate rural demand).
** Foreign direct investments and approvals are on an upswing.
** Industrial production is expected to pick-up in second half.
** Political developments are reducing the influence of the Communist parties on the direction of government policies.
NEGATIVE FACTORS as far as the market is concerned are:
** Government under pressure to expedite disinvestment programme/fund raising for PSEs - this will lead to larger supply in the primary market than we have seen in the earlier part of the year.

** Small investors are still averse to equities and are unlikely to return very quickly; issues that are dominating their minds are of corporate governance (following enforcement crackdowns on large companies) and possibility of further losses on small stocks following UTI's indication that they will consolidate their investments.
** No improvement in fiscal deficit control measures; the government's record on controlling subsidies and government expenditure is poor.
** Infrastructural bottlenecks, in particular power supply, could place pressure on growth rate.
On balance conditions are ambient for greater allocations to Indian equities by foreign investors and market revival from the current levels.
